{{Short description|American academic}}
{{Use mdy dates|date=November 2020}}
'''Peter L. Hagelstein''' is an associate professor of electrical engineering at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] (MIT), affiliated with the [[Research Laboratory of Electronics]] (RLE).

Hagelstein received a B.S. and M.S. in 1976 and Ph.D. in electrical engineering in 1981, from MIT.

Hagelstein began his career at the [[Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory]], working on high-energy laser and plasma physics from 1981 to 1985. While working in the Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, he pioneered the work that later produced the first X-ray laser, which would later become important for the US [[Strategic Defense Initiative]], popularly referred to as the "Star Wars" program.<ref>{{cite book|author=William J. Broad|title=Star warriors: a penetrating look into the lives of the young scientists behind our space age weaponry|year=1985|publisher=Simon and Schuster|isbn=978-0-671-54566-6}}</ref> His work on X-ray lasers was honored with the [[Ernest Orlando Lawrence Award]] in 1984. Following this time, he took up an academic appointment at MIT in 1986.

In 1989, he started investigating [[cold fusion]] (also called ''low-energy nuclear reactions'') with the hope of making a breakthrough similar to the X-ray laser.<ref name=daley2004/> In the period between 1989 and 2004, the field became discredited in the eyes of many scientists.<ref name=daley2004>{{citation |title= Heating up a cold theory |author= Beth Daley |work= The Boston Globe |date= July 27, 2004 |url= http://archive.boston.com/news/globe/health_science/articles/2004/07/27/heating_up_a_cold_theory/ |url-access=subscription }}</ref> Hagelstein continued his research activity in the field, chairing the Tenth [[International Conference on Cold Fusion]] in 2003.<ref>{{cite web | last = Hecht| first = Jeff | title = Is Cold Fusion Heating Up? | work = Technology Review | publisher = MIT | date = April 23, 2004 | url = http://www.technologyreview.com/energy/13559/page1/| accessdate = April 6, 2011}}</ref> On November 14, 2017, he gave a 90-minute presentation reviewing relevant experiments and describing possible mechanisms.<ref>{{cite web | last = Hagelstein| first = Peter | title = Cold Fusion - Real, But Is It Ready? | publisher = MIT Club of Northern California | date = November 17, 2017 | url = https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CiNDqaFPO4A | accessdate = June 17, 2021}}</ref>

Following the cold fusion episode, his primary research has shifted to solid-state physics, including the development of new [[thermoelectric materials]].<ref>{{cite news|title=A Practical Way to Make Power From Wasted Heat|last=Chang|first=Kenneth|date=November 27, 2001|newspaper=[[The New York Times]]|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2001/11/27/business/technology-a-practical-way-to-make-power-from-wasted-heat.html}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://web.mit.edu/newsoffice/2009/thermoelectric.html|title=Turning heat to electricity|last=Chandler|first=David L.|publisher=[[MIT]]|date=November 18, 2009|accessdate=July 17, 2014}}</ref> In addition, he is active in education, writing a textbook on quantum and statistical mechanics.
